Editor's note: Campbell Brown anchors CNN's "Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull" at 8 p.m. ET Mondays through Fridays. She delivered this commentary during the "Cutting through the Bull" segment of Monday night's broadcast. CNN's Campbell Brown says nonemergency legislation needs time to be read by the public and Congress. (CNN) -- Whether by omission or commission, both the White House and Congress get a dose of blame for not living up to the new era of transparency promised by President Obama. The president's old campaign Web site still has this commitment there for all to see: . "As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House Web site for five days." Well, the president broke that promise barely a week after taking office when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill dealing with equal pay for men and women. A good bill, and certainly one that could have survived a five-day comment period. So, maybe the White House folks just forgot? But then there is Congress and the Stimulus Bill. How fast could you get through it? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers had just 13 hours to read 1,100 pages of material that would cost the American taxpayer $787 billion. That's less than a minute and a half per page, with no time for bathroom breaks. No wonder so many of our lawmakers didn't seem to notice that last-minute exemption clearing the way for bailed-out companies like AIG to pay out big bonuses. So, the House tried to clean up the mess last week by rushing through another bill -- a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill was just 11 hours old before it went on the floor to be argued and then quickly approved. And the list goes on well before the president took office. The bank bailout got all of 29 hours, the rescue of Fannie and Freddie was only available for 19 hours. This is how bills could literally become, to borrow a phrase, too big to fail -- and too fast to stop. The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to allow the American people three days, 72 hours, to read a nonemergency bill online before debate begins. We strongly agree. And yes lawmakers, you can have three days to read it over, too, before taking a stand. As for President Obama's promise of a five-day public review once a bill leaves Capitol Hill headed for his desk, it would be nice if he kept his word on this going forward. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.

# Polished Version

**Editor's note:** *Campbell Brown anchors CNN's "Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull" weeknights at 8 p.m. ET. She delivered this commentary during the "Cutting through the Bull" segment of Monday night's broadcast.*

CNN's Campbell Brown argues that nonemergency legislation deserves adequate time for review by both the public and Congress.

(CNN) -- Whether through oversight or deliberate action, both the White House and Congress bear responsibility for falling short of the transparency President Obama promised. His campaign website still bears this pledge for all to see: "As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House website for five days."

Yet the president broke that promise barely a week into his term, signing the Lilly Ledbetter Act—legislation addressing equal pay for men and women—without the pledged waiting period. It was a worthy bill, one that surely could have withstood five days of public scrutiny. Perhaps it simply slipped the administration's mind.

Congress, however, offers no such excuse when it comes to the stimulus bill. Consider the pace at which lawmakers were expected to digest it: according to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, members of Congress had just 13 hours to review 1,100 pages of legislation carrying a $787 billion price tag for American taxpayers. That amounts to less than 90 seconds per page—hardly enough time for a bathroom break, let alone careful deliberation. Little wonder, then, that so many lawmakers failed to notice the last-minute exemption that cleared the way for bailed-out firms like AIG to distribute massive bonuses.

In an attempt to contain the fallout, the House rushed through a follow-up measure last week: a tax targeting AIG bonuses. That bill existed for a mere 11 hours before reaching the floor for debate and swift approval.

This pattern predates the current administration. The bank bailout bill was available for just 29 hours before passage; the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac rescue package, a scant 19 hours. This is precisely how legislation becomes—to borrow a phrase—too big to fail, and too fast to stop.

The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to guarantee the American public 72 hours to review any nonemergency bill online before debate commences. We wholeheartedly support this proposal. And yes, lawmakers deserve those same three days to study the legislation before casting their votes.

As for President Obama's pledge of a five-day public comment period once a bill reaches his desk, it would serve him well to honor that commitment moving forward.

*The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.*

# Broken Promises: Transparency Failures in Washington's Legislative Process

During his campaign for the presidency, Barack Obama made a specific and notable commitment to government transparency. His campaign website explicitly stated that as president, he would not sign any non-emergency legislation without first providing the American public a full five days to review the bill and submit comments through the White House website. This pledge was meant to signal a break from the closed-door dealings that had long characterized Washington politics, offering citizens a genuine opportunity to scrutinize legislation before it became law.

However, this promise proved short-lived. Just one week into his presidency, Obama signed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act without honoring the five-day public comment period he had promised. While the bill itself addressed an important issue—pay equity—the manner in which it was signed represented an early and telling departure from the transparency standards he had set for his own administration.

Congress, too, failed to meet reasonable standards of transparency and deliberation. The Stimulus Bill, a massive piece of legislation totaling 1,100 pages and carrying a price tag of $787 billion, was given to lawmakers with only 13 hours to read before they were required to vote on it. Given the sheer size and complexity of the bill, this timeframe made thorough review nearly impossible for any legislator, regardless of diligence or staff support.

This rushed timeline may well explain one of the more controversial oversights embedded in the bill: a last-minute provision that exempted certain bailed-out companies, including AIG, from restrictions on executive bonuses. This exemption allowed AIG to distribute substantial bonus payments to executives despite the company having received billions in taxpayer-funded assistance. The public backlash that followed raised serious questions about how such a provision could have been included and gone unnoticed—questions that are more easily answered when one considers that lawmakers had barely half a day to digest over a thousand pages of legislative text.

Unfortunately, this pattern of rushed review was not an isolated incident. Other major financial bills faced similarly compressed timelines. The bank bailout legislation was reviewed for just 29 hours before passage, while the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac rescue package received only 19 hours of consideration. In each case, lawmakers were asked to vote on bills with enormous financial implications—bills that would commit hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars—without adequate time to understand their full contents.

Taken together, these examples paint a troubling picture of how significant legislation is often processed in Washington. Whether through executive action or congressional votes, the pattern of compressed timelines for reviewing complex, high-stakes bills raises legitimate concerns about the quality of oversight being applied. When lawmakers themselves lack sufficient time to read and understand legislation before voting on it, the public is left to wonder how effectively their representatives can identify problematic provisions, unintended consequences, or hidden giveaways buried within the text. The gap between promised transparency and actual practice—evident in both the executive and legislative branches—suggests that meaningful reform of the legislative process may be necessary to ensure that speed does not continue to come at the expense of careful, informed governance.

# The Erosion of Legislative Transparency: A Pattern of Broken Promises

Time and again, both the White House and Congress have made solemn pledges to the American people about transparency in the legislative process, only to abandon those commitments when political expediency demands speed over scrutiny. This recurring failure has become a defining characteristic of how major legislation gets passed in Washington, with consequences that ripple far beyond simple procedural violations.

The pattern is strikingly consistent across multiple pieces of landmark legislation. Consider the economic stimulus bill, one of the most consequential pieces of legislation in recent memory, involving hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars. Despite promises that the public and lawmakers would have adequate time to review such significant spending measures, the bill—spanning approximately 1,100 pages—was rushed through with lawmakers given a mere 13 hours to read and comprehend its contents before voting. This timeline made it virtually impossible for any legislator, let alone their staff or the public, to fully understand the implications of what they were voting on.

Similarly, the AIG bonus tax legislation, crafted in the heat of public outrage over executive compensation at a bailed-out company, followed the same troubling pattern. Rather than allowing for careful deliberation and public input, the bill was fast-tracked through Congress, sacrificing thorough review for the appearance of swift action. The financial bailout legislation more broadly has suffered from this same affliction, with massive sums of taxpayer money being allocated through processes that bypassed the careful oversight that such significant expenditures warrant.

This rush to legislate carries serious consequences that extend well beyond the optics of broken promises. When lawmakers don't have sufficient time to actually read and analyze the bills they're voting on, critical details can slip through unnoticed—sometimes with significant financial or policy implications. The now-infamous AIG bonus loophole serves as a prime example of this danger. Buried within complex legislative language, this provision escaped scrutiny during the rushed review process, ultimately allowing the very bonuses that had sparked public fury to proceed largely unimpeded.

This pattern raises fundamental questions about accountability in the legislative process. If lawmakers cannot adequately review legislation before voting on it, how can they be expected to identify problematic provisions, understand unintended consequences, or ensure that the bills truly serve the public interest? The compressed timelines don't just inconvenience legislators—they fundamentally undermine the democratic process by preventing meaningful deliberation, public input, and the identification of provisions that may benefit special interests at the public's expense.

The repeated nature of these transparency failures suggests this isn't merely an occasional lapse but rather a systemic problem in how major legislation gets crafted and passed in times of perceived urgency. Whether driven by genuine crisis, political pressure, or simply institutional habit, this rush to legislate first and understand later represents a significant departure from the promises of open, transparent governance that both the executive branch and Congress have repeatedly made to the American public.

# CNN "No Bias, No Bull" - Commentary Transcript
## Campbell Brown

---Here's an original transcript in this style:

---

Tonight, I want to talk about something that should make every American uncomfortable, regardless of which side of the aisle you sit on.

We keep hearing this word—transparency. Candidate Obama promised it. President Obama has repeated it. Congress loves to say it too. But saying a word and actually living by it? Those are two very different things.

Let's talk about how the stimulus bill actually got passed. A trillion-dollar spending package—the largest in American history—and members of Congress had what, thirteen hours to read it before voting? Thousands of pages, drafted in backroom negotiations, dropped on lawmakers' desks in the middle of the night, with a vote scheduled before the sun even came up.

Now ask yourself—do you really believe every member of Congress read that bill? Do you believe they understood every provision, every earmark, every consequence buried in that legislation? Because I don't. And if they didn't have time to read it, how exactly were the American people supposed to weigh in on how their money was being spent?

This isn't a Democrat problem or a Republican problem. This is a Washington problem. We saw the same thing with TARP under the Bush administration. Rushed. Panicked. Passed with promises of oversight that somehow never quite materialized the way they were sold.

And now we're watching it happen again with this AIG bonus tax.

Everyone in Washington is falling over themselves this week to express outrage—real or manufactured—over these bonuses. Fine. The public anger is legitimate. A hundred and sixty-five million dollars in bonuses paid out by a company that exists only because taxpayers bailed it out? That's infuriating.

But watch what Congress did in response. In the span of just a few days, the House passed a bill to tax those bonuses at 90 percent. Almost no debate. Little discussion about the legal or constitutional questions raised by writing a tax code provision that appears to target specific individuals at a specific company. No real conversation about whether this sets a precedent that should concern every American, regardless of how you feel about AIG executives.

I'm not defending those bonuses. I think they were outrageous, and the retention agreements that protected them should have been renegotiated the moment taxpayer money entered the picture. But when Congress can turn around and pass sweeping punitive legislation in days—when they can't be bothered to spend that same urgency reviewing a trillion-dollar spending bill—you have to ask what's really driving these decisions.

Is it good policy? Or is it good politics? Because those aren't always the same thing.

Here's my problem with all of this: When you rush legislation—whether it's a stimulus package or a punitive tax bill—you sacrifice scrutiny. You sacrifice the ability of the public, of journalists, of independent experts to weigh in before the ink is dry. And you allow politicians to hide behind the size and complexity of these bills rather than actually answering for what's inside them.

The President promised us a new era of accountability. He talked about posting bills online for five days before signing them so the public could review them. That promise didn't survive first contact with the stimulus bill. And I haven't heard much about it since.

Washington loves a crisis. Crises create urgency, and urgency creates cover. Cover to push through legislation that might not survive the light of day if people actually had time to read it, question it, and hold their elected officials accountable for it.

We deserve better than this. Not because transparency is some abstract, feel-good value—but because in a democracy, an informed public is the entire point. If our government moves too fast for us to understand what it's doing with our money, then we've lost something fundamental about how this system is supposed to work.

I'm Campbell Brown. That's what I think. Tell me what you think—the conversation continues online.

---
*[END SEGMENT]*

# "Cutting Through the Bull" 
### Segment Script — CNN

---

**[CAMPBELL BROWN, seated at anchor desk, direct to camera]**

Alright, time to cut through the bull.

Remember this promise? "No more legislation that Congress hasn't had a chance to read." That was candidate Obama. That was the campaign trail. That was supposed to be different.

Remember this one? Five days. Every bill posted online for five days before a vote, so the American people — you — could actually see what's in it before your representatives vote on it.

So here's the bull. That's not happening. It hasn't been happening. And both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue are responsible.

**[Graphic: "5-DAY PROMISE" with a red X]**

We've watched major bills — spending packages, healthcare provisions, you name it — get dropped at midnight and voted on by noon. Thousands of pages. Nobody reads a thousand pages in twelve hours. Not you, not me, and let's be honest — not most of the people voting on it either.

The White House says it supports transparency. Congress says it supports transparency. Everybody supports transparency — right up until transparency is inconvenient. Right up until there's a deadline, a shutdown looming, a vote count that might fall apart if people have time to actually read what's inside.

**[Leans in]**

Here's the bull, plain and simple: this isn't about complexity. It's not that these bills are just *too complicated* to post in advance. It's that leadership — in both parties, under this administration and the last fight over the last big bill — likes rushing things through. Less time to read means less time to organize opposition. Less time for you to call your senator and say, "wait, what is THIS?"

**[Camera pushes in slightly]**

And spare me the excuses about "emergency" legislation. Some things are genuine emergencies. Most of what gets jammed through under that label isn't. It's just bad planning dressed up as urgency.

So here's what we're going to keep doing on this show: every time a bill gets dropped with no real chance for the public — or frankly, half of Congress — to read it, we're going to call it out. By name. By bill number. Because "trust us" is not a substitute for transparency.

**[Beat, softer tone]**

Look — I'm not naive. Governing is messy. Deadlines are real. But the five-day promise wasn't a suggestion. It was a commitment. And broken commitments, especially about how our laws get made, deserve exactly this kind of scrutiny.

That's the bull. We'll keep cutting.

**[Cut to break]**

---

*[Segment runtime: ~90 seconds]*

# News Commentary Transcript

**[EDITOR'S NOTE: The following is a transcript excerpt from a Campbell Brown program segment. Campbell Brown hosted a nightly news commentary show that focused on political accountability, examining the gap between campaign rhetoric and governing reality. This particular segment addressed a specific promise made during the 2008 presidential campaign.]**

---

**CAMPBELL BROWN:** Good evening. Tonight we're looking at a promise made, and a promise broken.

Back on the campaign trail in 2008, then-Senator Obama made a pledge that resonated with a lot of Americans frustrated with how Washington does business. He said that before signing any non-emergency bill, he would post it online for five days, giving the public a chance to actually read it, weigh in, and hold their representatives accountable before it became law.

It was a small promise, in the scheme of things. But it spoke to something bigger—this idea of transparency, of pulling back the curtain on a legislative process that often moves too fast for anyone outside the Beltway to track.

So how's that promise holding up?

Not well.

Look at the stimulus bill—over a thousand pages, negotiated behind closed doors, and voted on almost immediately after being finalized. Members of Congress themselves admitted they hadn't read the whole thing. The health care legislation followed a similar pattern—massive, complex bills, released to the public with barely enough time to skim the table of contents, let alone understand the implications, before votes were cast.

This isn't a partisan critique. This is a process critique. When bills reshaping a sixth of the American economy or committing trillions in spending are rushed through in a matter of days—sometimes hours—the five-day rule isn't just being bent. It's being ignored.

The White House has offered various justifications—economic emergencies, procedural technicalities, the difference between "the bill" and "the final bill." But for the millions of Americans who heard that promise and believed it meant something, those explanations ring hollow.

The question isn't really about one administration or one party. It's about whether campaign promises about process and transparency mean anything once the votes are counted and the governing begins.

We'll be joined after the break by two guests who'll debate whether this broken promise matters—or whether it's simply the reality of how Washington has always worked, dressed up in new rhetoric.

Stay with us.

---

*[END OF TRANSCRIPT EXCERPT]*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an opinion segment in the voice of a CNN political anchor arguing that Congress and the president have failed to give citizens adequate time to review major legislation like the stimulus and bailout bills.
counterfactuals.output:
**[OPINION SEGMENT — CNN STYLE]**

"You know, there's a principle that most of us learn early on—whether it's signing a mortgage, a business contract, or even a lease for an apartment: you read it before you sign it. You take the time. You ask questions. You don't just take someone's word for what's in the fine print.

And yet, time and again, we've watched Congress and the White House—regardless of which party holds the pen—rush trillion-dollar bills through the legislative process with barely enough time for lawmakers themselves to read them, let alone the American people who'll be paying for them for generations.

Think about it: these bills often run into the hundreds, sometimes thousands of pages. They're released publicly sometimes just hours—hours—before a vote. Lawmakers are asked to vote on legislation that shapes housing policy, banking regulation, unemployment benefits, tax law—major, structural decisions—without adequate time to consult experts, hear from constituents, or even fully grasp what's being proposed.

Now, defenders of this approach will say: 'We're in a crisis. Markets are collapsing. Families are struggling. We don't have the luxury of time.' And look, that's a fair point when we're talking about hours or days of delay in a genuine emergency. But when 'emergency' becomes the default justification for every major piece of legislation—stimulus bills, bailout packages, appropriations—it starts to look less like urgency and more like avoidance. Avoidance of scrutiny. Avoidance of debate. Avoidance of accountability.

Because here's the thing about transparency: it's not just a bureaucratic nicety. It's the mechanism by which democracy actually works. When citizens can't see what's in a bill until after it's law, they can't weigh in. They can't call their representatives with informed questions. They can't hold anyone accountable for specific provisions—because nobody had time to identify what those provisions even were.

There have been proposals—some quite reasonable—for a simple rule: publish the text of major legislation 72 hours before a vote. Give the public, and frankly give Congress itself, a chance to actually read what they're about to commit trillions of dollars to. It's not a radical idea. It's not partisan. It's just... basic due diligence.

The people footing the bill for these programs—today's taxpayers and tomorrow's—deserve more than a rushed news cycle and a hastily called press conference. They deserve a legislative process that respects their right to understand what's being done in their name.

Because in the end, speed is not the same as urgency, and secrecy is not the same as efficiency. If we want to rebuild public trust in Washington, it starts with something as fundamental as this: let the public read the bill."
